about: Implementation 04-3, Phase 2: the gallery of patterns. One pattern, one name: Phase 3 uses these ids and levels in the level prompts. Images are relative to this folder (drawn/) or to context/implementations/04-app-enhancements/images/chopin_passages/. pdf pages are pages of the user's PDFs in /home/david/Documents/projects/music/chopin/ (outside the repo). kern files are in poc-aitu-research/data/raw/kern/humdrum-chopin-first-editions/kern/.
status: proposed, waiting for the user's review

patterns.name: Slow melody in single notes
patterns.line: Si4 held for three beats, then Do5: the melody alone, with long notes and no chords. Easy because the hand has one note at a time and almost no movement.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 4

patterns.name: Melody in single notes
patterns.line: Fa#5-Sol5-Fa#5-Do#5-Re5-Si4 in corcheas, then La#4: one line of single notes inside one hand position. Easy because there are no chords, also when the notes are corcheas.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 69 No. 2

patterns.name: A second note on long notes
patterns.line: Single notes on the short figures, and a second note (a third, a sixth) only on the long ones; three notes only to land on a long note. Medium because the hand stays fluent and the chords come when there is time for them.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 64 No. 2
examples.note: Sol#4-Mi5 held as a sixth, then Fa##4-Re#5.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23
examples.note: Two notes on the blancas with puntillo, single notes on the negras, three notes to land on bar 70 (the user's example of page 10).

patterns.name: Melody in chords, one rhythm
patterns.line: The melody on top of three-note chords on every negra, with the same rhythm (corchea with puntillo, semicorchea, two negras) every two bars. Hard because every note is a chord, although the rhythm repeats and the tempo is slow.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 7

patterns.name: Melody with small pieces of chords
patterns.line: The melody on top (Sib5, Lab5, Solb5) with a second voice and two-note pieces of chords under it, and a few decoration notes. Hard because the hand plays the melody and part of the harmony (the brief's example of Ballade No. 4).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Melody over an inner line
patterns.line: The melody in negras with puntillo on the fifth finger, and a line of corcheas under it in the same hand. Hard because one hand plays two voices with different rhythms.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 42

patterns.name: Thirds and sixths in corcheas
patterns.line: Two notes on every corchea (Fa5-Reb5, Mib5-Sol4) after a long two-note chord. Hard because the hand plays double notes fast, although it keeps the same shape.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 70 No. 3

patterns.name: Full chords in octaves
patterns.line: Chords of four and five notes, ff, with the melody doubled at the octava and jumps up of an octave (La4-Do#5-La5, then La5-Do#6-La6). Super hard because the hand is open to its limit and jumps.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Runs in groups of 7 and 8
patterns.line: Fast runs of semicorcheas in groups of 7 and 8 that cross positions, over the left hand's sweeps. Super hard because the hand moves without rest and both hands move at once.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Held triad
patterns.line: The chord of the harmony (Fa-La-Do) held under the melody; the hand changes position only when the harmony changes. Easy because the hand holds one shape and does not move inside the chord.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then the chord
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4: one note and one chord, the same shape every time. Easy because the hand makes one jump of an octave to a triad that does not change.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triads in steps
patterns.line: The triad slides one step up or down with the melody (Fa-La-Do, Sol-Sib-Re, La-Do-Mi). Easy because the three fingers keep one shape and the hand moves one key at a time.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held chord, repeated
patterns.line: A small chord held as a blanca and played again with the same notes, bar after bar. Easy because the hand does not move at all.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Low note, then two notes rocking
patterns.line: Fa2, then La3-Do4-La3-Do4 in corcheas: one low note, then two notes of the chord one after the other. Easy because after the low note the hand stays on two keys.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Alberti bass
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4-La3-Do4 in corcheas, again and again: the lowest, the highest and the middle note of the triad. Easy because the hand never leaves the position of the triad.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-La3 in corcheas: the three notes of the chord going up and coming down. Easy because the figure is symmetric and stays in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad up, then held
patterns.line: Fa3 and La3 in corcheas, then Do4 as a negra: the triad goes up and stops on its top note. Easy because three fingers stay on three keys.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad down, then held
patterns.line: Do4 and La3 in corcheas, then Fa3 as a negra: the same figure going down. Easy for the same reason as going up.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Chord, then two notes above
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4, then Do4-Fa4: the chord, then two of its notes in a higher position, again and again. Easy because the hand moves a little and comes back, always with the same two shapes.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held two-note chord
patterns.line: The fifth Fa3-Do4 held as blancas (Do3-Sol3 and Sib2-Fa3 for the other chords). Easy because two notes are enough to give the harmony and the hand holds one shape.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then two-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2, then La3-Do4 three times in negras. Easy because the chord has only two notes and its shape never changes.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Two-note chord, then an arpeggio
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4 together, then Fa3-La3-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3 in corcheas. Easy because the arpeggio uses the same position as the two-note chord.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Fifth to sixth, rocking
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4, then Fa3-Re4, in negras: the upper note moves one key and back while the lower note stays. Easy because only one finger moves.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then the octave
patterns.line: Mi2, then the octave Mi3-Mi4 on the two next beats, in a slow tempo. Medium because of the octava; the jump and the shape are the same in every bar.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 7

patterns.name: Low note, then two chords
patterns.line: The waltz left hand: a low note on the first beat, then the same chord on the second and third beats. Medium because the hand jumps every bar, but the chord shape stays and only the bass note changes.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 69 No. 2
examples.note: Si2, then Fa#3-Si3-Re4 twice: the plain pattern.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 64 No. 3
examples.note: Lab2, Mib2, Lab2 under the same chord Mib3-Lab3-Do4: only the fifth finger moves.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 64 No. 2
examples.note: Do#2, then Sol#3-Do#4-Mi4: the same pattern with a jump of more than an octave, the hardest form of it.

patterns.name: Held bass under two chords
patterns.line: The low note is held for the whole bar (blanca with puntillo) while two chords sound on the second and third beats. Medium because there is no jump: the hand stays over the bass and the chord.

examples.piece: Waltz Op. 69 No. 1

patterns.name: Low note, then two chords, in corcheas
patterns.line: Mib2, then two chords in beamed corcheas (Sol3-Mib4, then Sib3-Mib4-Sol4), three times in a bar. Medium because the figure repeats at every beat; the second chord only adds a note on top.

examples.piece: Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2

patterns.name: Same chord, one note changes
patterns.line: One chord repeated in corcheas (Sol3-Si3-Mi4); every bar or half bar one or two of its notes move down (Fa#3-La3-Mi4, then Fa#3-La3-Mib4, then Fa3-La3-Mib4). Medium because of the many notes, but the hand never leaves its position.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 4

patterns.name: Repeated note
patterns.line: Lab3 repeated in corcheas, with a low note and a small chord on the strong beats. Medium because the thumb stays on one key and the other fingers add the harmony.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 15

patterns.name: Octave bass in negras
patterns.line: Octavas in negras that walk down by semitones (Do, Si, Sib, La, Lab, Sol). Medium because the hand keeps the octave shape and slides; it gives a strong bass without more notes.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 20

patterns.name: Low note, then a small wave
patterns.line: Fa#2, then Mi#3-Sol#3-Fa#3-La#3 and back to Do#3: a low note and a short figure up and down inside one hand position, the same at every half bar. Medium because the figure never changes.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 13

patterns.name: Simple line in negras
patterns.line: Single notes in negras: a low note, then a broken chord that climbs, with a step or two between its notes (Sib1, Sib2, Lab3, Fa3, Do4, Sib3). Medium because there are few notes and they are easy to read, although they belong to no fixed shape (the user's example of page 10).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Octava, then an arpeggio
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3 together, then Fa3-La3-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3 in corcheas. Medium because of the octava and the jump to the arpeggio; the arpeggio itself stays in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then chords off the beat
patterns.line: Fa2 on the beat, then the triad on the half beats (corcheas), with blank space between them. Medium because of the rhythm: the chord sounds between the beats.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Added sixth, up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Re4 and back in corcheas: the triad with its sixth (Re), a new note of the chord. Medium because the hand uses four fingers, still in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held bass under rocking notes
patterns.line: Fa3 held for the whole bar while La3-Do4 rock above it in corcheas. Medium because one hand plays two voices: one finger holds and the others move.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-La3 in semicorcheas at every beat. Medium because the notes are fast, although the figure and the position never change.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octava, then two beamed chords
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then the triad twice in beamed corcheas, twice in each bar (the brief's example of an octava and two corcheas of the chord). Medium because of the jump between the octava and the chord.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Alternating bass and chord
patterns.line: Fa2, the triad, Do3, the triad, in negras: the bass changes between the root and the fifth of the chord. Medium because the bass note moves every two beats.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Arpeggio in 3 + 3 + 2
patterns.line: The triad in corcheas grouped 3 + 3 + 2 (Fa3-La3-Do4, Fa3-La3-Do4, Fa3-La3), a common rhythm in pop songs. Medium because the groups do not follow the beat, although the notes stay in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octavas rocking
patterns.line: Fa2, Fa3, Fa2, Fa3 in corcheas: the octava played as two notes, one after the other. Medium because the hand stays open on the octava for the whole bar.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Chord, then an arpeggio down
patterns.line: The triad, then Fa4-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3-Do4 in corcheas: down from the top and back. Medium because the arpeggio covers an octava, one note more than the triad.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octave, then the chord up and down
patterns.line: The octava Mi1-Mi2, then the chord in negras going up and coming down with the same notes. Hard because the hand jumps and changes fingers, but the way down repeats the way up (the user's example of page 12).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Low note, then a chord that moves
patterns.line: Fa3, then Reb4-Mi4-Sol4 and the same shape one step lower (Sib3-Reb4-Mi4); then Fa2, Do4-Fa4-Lab4 and Lab3-Do4-Fa4. Hard because the second chord moves (the brief's hard level) and the hand crosses from the bass to the treble clef.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Octaves that draw the chord
patterns.line: Octavas in corcheas that go through the notes of the chord (Solb, Reb, Solb, Sib, Mib, Sib) under held chords of the right hand. Hard because the hand moves on every note, but it keeps the octave shape and a regular figure.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Wave in one position
patterns.line: A low note, then semicorcheas in groups of six that go up and come down over the chord (Dob2, then Dob3-Reb3-Fa3-Reb4-Fa3-Reb3). Hard because they are fast, but each wave is symmetric and the hand stays over one place.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: A line that belongs to no chord
patterns.line: A low note, then two-note chords in corcheas whose notes move apart, the lower one down by semitones and the upper one up (Mi3-Sol3, Mib3-La3, Re3-Sib3, Do3-Do4). Hard because the line fits no known chord (the brief's irregular passages), but the hand stays in one position.

examples.piece: Prelude Op. 28 No. 21

patterns.name: Four-note arpeggio up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 and back in corcheas: the triad with its octava as a fourth note. Hard because the hand is open on the octava and uses all five fingers.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then four-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 three times in negras. Hard because the chord fills the octava and the hand jumps to it.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Open arpeggio up and down
patterns.line: Fa2-Do3-Fa3-La3-Do4 and back in corcheas: the root, the fifth, the octava and the tenth. Hard because the arpeggio covers more than an octava and the hand must move inside it.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Alberti over an octava
patterns.line: Fa3-Fa4-Do4-Fa4, La3-Fa4-Do4-Fa4: the Alberti figure with the octava on top. Hard because the hand stays open on the octava while the lower fingers change.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Four-note wave in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 up and down in semicorcheas. Hard because the wave is fast and covers an octava; it is symmetric, so the fingers repeat.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octava, then a chord that moves up
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then Fa3-La3-Do4 and La3-Do4-Fa4 in corcheas: the second chord is the same chord one position higher (the brief's La4-Do5-Mi5, then Do5-Mi5-La5). Hard because the hand moves between the two chords.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octava, then four-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 six times in corcheas. Hard because the hand jumps and then repeats a full chord fast.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held bass under moving thirds
patterns.line: Fa3 held, with La3-Do4 and Sib3-Re4 moving above it in corcheas. Hard because one hand plays two voices and the upper voice moves two fingers at a time.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Four-note chords off the beat
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3 on the beat, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 on the half beats. Hard because of the jump, the full chord and the rhythm between the beats.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Arpeggio up, then the chord
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 in corcheas, then the four notes together as a blanca. Hard because the hand covers the octava twice, first note by note and then all at once.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Sweeps over two octaves
patterns.line: From Fa2 up to Lab4 in six semicorcheas, twice in each bar, then a jump back down. Super hard because the hand opens, crosses and jumps without rest while the right hand runs in groups of 7 and 8.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Fast octaves in stretto
patterns.line: A chord, then octavas in corcheas (Dob, Sib, Do, Sib), faster and faster (stretto), under chords of four notes that jump in the right hand. Super hard because both hands play heavy shapes at speed.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
